speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head O of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I know of a man, now in his 70s, who had been smoking since his teens.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: No amount of persuasion, threats, nicotine patches or counseling could make him quit.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And then, he was hospitalised for a minor heart attack a few years ago, and he has not smoked since.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I know of a woman, also in her 70s, who cares about so many people around her, but despite her advancing years somehow never got around to going for health screening, despite the urging of her family, and although she herself would urge her family to go for regular health checks.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And then, one day, her group of friends decided to go for a health check at the nearby polyclinic, and because it was their regular meet-up for lunch, she decided to just tag along, had the very first mammogram of her life, which detected very early stage breast cancer, which was then quickly and safely removed.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Much has been written on how one’s attitudes to health and health seeking behavior can be changed.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It can be due to some catastrophic event, such as the onset of disease, but in the absence of such event, what else can be done to nudge someone towards better health practices?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: You would think that any reasonable person would take the appropriate steps to stay healthy, but we smoke, we drink more than we should, we eat too much, exercise not too much, and so on.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We emphasise health education, we try to "game-ify" healthy practices, such as the 10,000 step challenge.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Against tobacco, we have cornered the industry at every turn, short of an outright ban.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But still, ill health in our society remains frustratingly, maddeningly sticky.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some years ago, I was proud to mention that Singapore was the Healthiest Country in the World.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In terms of healthcare, the system in Singapore remains affordable and accessible, and of very high quality.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But rightly, over the past few years, Singapore has shifted more and more resources towards health promotion and maintenance, rather than to costly medical services.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Part of the three key shifts are espoused by the Ministry of Health (MOH).

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe that choosing and maintaining healthy lifestyle choices can only be achieved if there is a community and whole-of-society approach, a support structure that positively reinforces such behavior.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just like recidivism among ex-offenders can only be drastically reduced by strong family and community support, many studies show that if we encourage one another at every opportunity, then we will find it easy to live healthily.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, we have to be healthy together, as it is difficult to stay the course alone.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We often go for health screenings on the encouragement of friends and loved ones, maintain our diets with the support of friends and family, and quit smoking when we want to do it for the betterment of both ourselves and our families.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is vitally important that the Government supports this whole-of-society effort.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I was very happy to learn of the new multi-agency task force that has been set up to drive health promotion.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand that “it will coordinate and synergise efforts across multiple public agencies, to nudge Singaporeans towards adopting a healthy lifestyle”.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With regard to diabetes, we are now in the third year of a long and bruising campaign against diabetes.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What milestones in our war on diabetes have been achieved?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is the Ministry still considering a tax on sugar?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore also hosted the inaugural Ministerial Conference on Diabetes in November of last year.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The conference brought together more than 300 international and local delegates, including health ministers, senior government officials, academics and thought leaders from 18 countries.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What are the takeaways from the inaugural Ministerial Conference on Diabetes in November last year?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Moving on to alcohol, concerning alcohol intake, I would like to follow up on a recent Parliamentary Question (PQ) I filed concerning recommendations about alcohol consumption.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A systematic analysis of scientific evidence that was published about alcohol in the Lancet in September last year, concluded that: "Alcohol use is a leading risk factor for disease burden worldwide, accounting for nearly 10% of global deaths among populations aged 15 to 49 years", very young, "and poses dire ramifications for future population health in the absence of policy action today.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The widely held view of the health benefits of alcohol needs revising, particularly as improved methods and analyses continue to show how much alcohol use contributes to global death and disability.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our results show that the safest level of drinking is none.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This level is in conflict with most health guidelines, which espouse health benefits associated with consuming up to two drinks a day".

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Regarding dementia, I note that there have been cuts filed on mental health.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I would like to ask about our national strategy to deal with dementia.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With longer lifespans and an ageing population, comes an increase in the number of patients with dementia.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is the progress on the expansion of dementia-friendly communities?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition to measures to curb sugar intake that are alluded to earlier, are there also efforts to reduce fat intake in our diet?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What about efforts to increase participation in regular exercise and sports?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Although heavily subsidised, many older Singaporeans, and many of them live in my constituency of Queenstown, still maintain the attitude that it is better not to know about their health conditions, or are concerned that screening examinations are too inconvenient, too difficult or too onerous for them.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is the latest step in the push to encourage preventive care.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is the proportion of adults who have had vaccinations since?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are we still seeing 100% coverage for children under the National Childhood Immunisation Programme?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I know that there have been cases of parents who have refused due to misconceptions about potential side effects of vaccinations for the children.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can MOH reach out to them and convince them of the benefits?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: One of the most important characteristics that keep us at the forefront is the ability to robustly adapt and be dynamic.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And this is unique in terms of healthcare because it is an area that is rapidly changing and developing.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is going to have to continue into the future.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I have five areas that we have to focus on moving ahead.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We have been reviewing our policies, we have been liberalising, we have been doing all kinds of things and tweaking according to the needs of our population as we move into the future.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We must review at regular intervals and we must make sure that we tweak accordingly and appropriately as well.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We need an adequate projection of numbers into the future of the pipeline for provision of care of the types of different healthcare personnel that we will need.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The demand will be high in an industry which is really labour-intensive.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our graduates from our traditional schools and institutions will continue to churn out numbers.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But the numbers will need tweaking as well and this will have to meet our demands.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Perhaps, also tapping on the retired personnel who are still healthy will be an option to consider moving into the future.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In terms of innovation and productivity, healthcare, as I said, is labour-intensive and patient-centric.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, we need to review that appropriately as well.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fifth, it is data-driven healthcare which is really a must moving into the future.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This will help us formulate guidelines and policies.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Key performance indicators must be reviewed regularly as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Ministry indicated that it would study my suggestion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Bukit Batok Single Member Constituency where I serve, residents have benefited from a range of in-patient services provided by St Luke’s Hospital, a community hospital dedicated to the elderly sick, over two decades.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The services extended by the hospital have increased significantly and now includes, in addition to medical care, palliative care, rehabilitation care and dementia care.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister responded in 2017 by stating that MediShield Life was designed to provide coverage for large acute hospital bills and there is a need to guard against cost escalation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would respectfully point out that there are benefits in right-siting the care of the patients at an appropriate healthcare institution so that precious resources in acute hospitals are not stretched.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for an update on this matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For the consumer, however, the current lack of regulation has meant that there is patchy information on available services and vastly different consumer experiences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the one hand, I have personally had good experiences with private ambulances.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, I hear less happy accounts from residents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such feedback includes high charges and a lack of advance disclosure or transparency about the costs of various services and equipment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Others include asking the family to decide if certain equipment should be used enroute which laypersons have little knowledge of.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another concern is that private ambulances attending cases at Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats may not have the stretchers that can be manoeuvred into an incline position to fit the size of HDB lifts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The quality of the vehicles is also disparate, with some ambulances apparently retrofitted from cargo vans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was recently reported that regulation is coming in the form of the proposed Healthcare Services Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While this is welcomed by consumers as well as industry players, there are some concerns.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The current proposal is that those licensed to provide emergency ambulance services would have more stringent requirements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, they will need to appoint a clinical director to maintain standards of comprehensive emergency care, to conduct audits, do training and protocol development.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, businesses which provide medical transport services in non-emergency cases do not need to meet the same standard but will have operational restrictions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, they will not be allowed to have blinkers and sirens.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Operators have pointed out that patients who are initially stable cases can deteriorate suddenly enroute to the hospital which will turn a non-emergency situation into an emergency one.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When this happens, time is of the essence and blinkers and sirens may make all the difference.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Mr Chairman, the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) programme, I am happy to note, has progressed significantly since its inception.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Today, the majority of general practitioner (GP) clinics support it.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: A new CHAS card for chronic disease management was announced by the Prime Minister last year and I would like to ask for more details about this new card.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: As the new card will cover all Singaporeans for chronic conditions, regardless of income, we can expect greater demand for the services of participating GPs.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Does the Ministry expect more GP clinics to join the network and can we look forward to a 100% participation rate?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: What are the obstacles that still prevent clinics from joining?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: What plans does MOH have to help them?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Given the rise in median household incomes over the years, I would also like to ask if the qualifying income criteria for the Blue and Orange CHAS cards will be revised and also if the benefits can be revised upwards, in addition to the new benefits announced, that is, the increased subsidies for complex chronic conditions and the extension of subsidies for common illnesses to Orange cardholders.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: MOH has also stated that it aims to strengthen the private primary healthcare sector.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: MOH started the Primary Care Network (PCN) scheme in January 2018, where GPs come together to provide holistic team-based care for their patients.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Would MOH please provide an update on this scheme?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: It was announced during the Budget Statement that the Ministry "will be looking at how to help CHAS clinics better track their patients' progress and outcomes".

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Can this tracking process also be enabled at the PCN level?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, personalised medicine involves the customisation of medical treatments to specific patient groups based on genetic profiles.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: At last year's MOH Committee of Supply (COS), I asked the Minister whether MOH was on track with drafting the code of practice for clinical genetic testing.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: First, precision medicine is a fast-developing field of clinical research and application.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I am concerned that the longer we take in enforcing the code of practice and implementing the national strategy, developments in the field would have outpaced the code and strategy.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Second, if a substantial number of Singaporeans have already obtained personalised medical treatments, then the delay in enforcing the code of practice may expose these Singaporeans to the misuse of their personal and deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) data, medical risks associated with DNA-editing and other bioethical risks.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: There was an international uproar and the Chinese Government is putting in a regulatory regime now in response.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I am concerned that the longer we take in regulating precision medicine and genetic testing, we may run the risk of such an incident happening here that will damage our reputation as a biomedical research and development hub.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the SingHealth cyberattack and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Registry leak have shaken confidence in the security of our personal and patient information and health records.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Learning from these events, how will the personal and patient data be kept in the National Electronic Health Record (NEHR) be better secured and protected against hacks and also leaks by administrators, doctors, finance staff and researchers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This negative sentiment preceded the SingHealth cyberattack and HIV Registry leak.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, the Government will need to get better buy-ins for NEHR from the public now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Should NEHR be minimally covered by the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) and the data protection regime that provides for additional safeguards and is patient-centric?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a move can improve public confidence as many are now familiar with the PDPA framework.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Small private clinics will need extra help to secure the data.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has been centralising patients' health records through the NEHR.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Patients can go to any healthcare facility and receive treatment that takes account of their medical history.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: However, the recent MOH data leaks and the cyberattack on SingHealth have shaken the public's confidence in such centralised electronic health records.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: These incidents targeting patients' personal records are reminders of the risks to privacy and security that accompany convenience, risks which we had not understood or taken seriously enough.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This has been held in abeyance while MOH does a thorough review of its cybersecurity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: However, even before the recent breaches, some GPs in private practice told me they had grave reservations about the impending requirement for them to key in confidential data about their patients into NEHR.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: They cited that they had a duty of doctor-patient confidentiality and were not comfortable keying in the medical conditions and drugs prescribed to patients, for review by unknown persons down the line.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In view of the potential for unauthorised access or leaks, they would also be reluctant to put in sensitive information, however relevant to treatment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: There is also the risk of disgruntled or rogue employees who can exploit legitimate access for improper purposes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: As it is impossible to completely prevent hacks and data breaches, one key concern would be to limit damage in the event of breaches.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: To mitigate the risks and fallout from data breaches, common and effective measures include improvements in ways to store and access information, such as data compartmentalisation and restrictions on authority.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: For instance, it would be odd for persons responsible for macro-level policy to access personally identifiable information.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It would also be unnecessary for staff not attending to a particular patient to access the patient’s records.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: There may be particular sensitivities if certain information gets into the wrong hands.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In view of all this, I would like to ask what MOH has done, or is doing, to compartmentalise data and limit who can gain access to data stored at MOH and at the healthcare providers it regulates.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is personal as it may contain information relating to medical conditions and diseases that the patient may want to keep private.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The release of this information could cause turmoil to the patient and his or her family, leading to serious stress in relationships.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To ensure information technology (IT) and cybersecurity specialists operating within the specialised sphere of medical information are trained well and that standards are kept high across health clusters and the many hospitals, would MOH consider setting up a Medical Cybersecurity Academy to train a core group of medical cybersecurity specialists share best practices among them and then steadily raise the industry standard, such as to protect medical records and the related information contained in them?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are on top of the universal Government subsidies available.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On top of these, the Government introduced different schemes to help Singaporeans, especially the elderly, better cope in their old age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singaporeans' average out-of-pocket expenditure, as a percentage of bill size, has also trended downwards.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some Singaporeans genuinely cannot afford it, some struggle to pay it off, and some do not even seek treatment because they do not know if they can afford it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For the low-income, they can apply for MediFund or public financial assistance if they pass the means test.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This will cover their medical expenses in public healthcare settings.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the course of my community work in MacPherson, I have met many low-income residents, especially the vulnerable elderly, receiving full medical coverage under such schemes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, for the average Singaporean, the ability to afford or continue to afford is less certain.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I would like to ask the Ministry how ready is an average Singaporean in coping with his/her healthcare cost, especially in old age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could the Ministry share the calculations and projections?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could the Ministry compare how an average retiree today and an average retiree in, say, 2030 or beyond, cope with their expected healthcare costs?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Is our current public healthcare financing method sustainable?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A recent feedback unit Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH) survey concluded incidents like the recent furore of MediShield Life not covering much of a certain bill, do not help.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some Singaporeans go to Johor Baru to purchase medication.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other than other pocket expenses, there is concern that premiums for MediShield Life and Integrated Shield Plans (IPs) may rise in future, thanks to healthcare inflation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Going forward, can we find cheaper ways to deliver the same healthcare outcomes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Value-based healthcare (VBH) which was conceptualised in the University of Utah in the United States (US), is a healthcare delivery model in which providers, including hospitals and doctors, are paid based on a patient's health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Value-based care differs from paying providers based on the amount of healthcare services they deliver.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While it is hard to summarise how this works in practice in under two minutes, it involves practices like sharing of data across physicians, to prevent redundant testing and adjusting payments to hospitals based on good care practices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While there have been trials by organisations, no national healthcare system has implemented VBH on a national level yet.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I understand that many companies are developing solutions for VBH in anticipation of an eventual VBH revolution in healthcare.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway and JP Morgan Chase have a joint venture to champion elements of VBH as a disruptive healthcare solution.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand that the National University Health System (NUHS) has adopted a value-driven outcome initiative.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: NUHS states that it drew the ideas of the VBH concept from the University of Utah and has shared the concept with public healthcare clusters in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, when is the target date for a more broad-based adoption of VBH and would a roadmap be published?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: However, this is very limiting for those with more than $20,000 in their MediSave Account.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This is especially if the long-term care is the only medical cost that they have to deal with, and that if the care is effective and preventive, it will minimise additional medical expenses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Why not peg the limit to the median duration instead?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The Government should consider increasing the maximum quantum to $600 and scale up according to the amount in the member's MediSave savings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: If the Member has $20,000 in his/her MediSave Account, he/she can draw up to $300 a month as $20,000 will cover 60 months of stay in a nursing home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: If the member has $40,000, he/she can withdraw up to $600 a month.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This may be a more efficient and effective way for severely disabled Singaporeans to make use of their MediSave savings to meet their long-term medical needs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For the second question, my reply would be, "Sorry, I do not have the answer." Therefore, Sir, I would like to ask the Ministry the following questions pertaining to MediSave withdrawal limits.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One, how is the withdrawal limit amount as well as the incremental amount being tabulated and arrived at?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Is there any specific formula applied and, if yes, can the Ministry share this formula?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Two, how regular is the review on the withdrawal limit conducted?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Is there any specific cycle or is it on situational basis, for example, review will be conducted when there is an inflation in the healthcare cost?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Third, who are involved in this reviewing process?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, it will provide some clarity and transparency on the matter.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Pritam Singh, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is particularly for bills which are not covered by MediShield Life or because the amount owing is within the deductible limit and, hence, must be settled solely by the patient in cash or MediSave.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In such cases, MediShield Life does not kick in because it is meant for larger hospital bills.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While MediSave can be used, it is subject to limits and, in many cases, a few hundred dollars will still have to coughed up in cash.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe there is scope for the Government to exercise some flexibility and give Singaporeans the choice of allowing the entire remaining amount after subsidies to be paid by a patient's MediSave instead of cash, bearing in mind the matter involves a hospitalisation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For citizens with sufficient MediSave balances, and who are in their senior years from the age of 60, in particular, some additional flexibility in terms of choice would bring significant peace of mind, leaving cash in their pocket.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Government can look into this to reduce the out-of-pocket expenses for this category of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, can the Government consider a tiered-withdrawal quantum for those above 60, not too dissimilar from the MediSave withdrawals for Long-Term Care announced in July last year to achieve a sustainable balance between the use of member's MediSave savings for the immediate term and the future respectively?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, Sir, CareShield Life and MediShield Life are both compulsory schemes, with the former soon to become a central pillar of our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The public cannot opt-out of either scheme, and this fact alone brings into sharp focus the premiums of compulsory risk-pooling schemes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would follow that the adequacy ratios of such schemes and the Government's reasons and assumptions behind premium pricing should be made more transparent so that the public can understand the factors behind premiums calculation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I appreciate that the actuarial models that determine how premiums are priced are complex and multifaceted.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some factors include disability mortality, recovery rate, claims continuance rate, improvements to mortality as well as the risk profiles of various cohorts, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, complexity should not be a reason to avoid publishing these considerations and the weightage of the calculations behind them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With the upcoming legislation of CareShield Life, I hope these assumptions and considerations can be meaningfully communicated to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On a similar note, I would like to enquire about the frequency with which MediShield Life's adequacy ratio is reviewed by the MediShield Life Council and considered by the Ministry, so as to ensure that the greater transparency on reserve requirements called for in the MediShield Life Review Committee report are meaningfully operationalised.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand the Frequently Asked Questions section on MediShield Life on the MOH website provides a helpful table, setting out the incurred loss ratio of the scheme each year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It also helps create peace of mind that all is done to ensure the affordability of these compulsory insurance schemes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the absence of such knowledge regarding spending, insurance may be inaccurately perceived by some as a pure tax, rather than a risk-pooling scheme that is closely tied to each participating cohorts' expected benefits.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Mr Chairman, arising from the feedback I received from Singaporeans who went through difficulties during and after giving birth to their baby, I had asked in October last year whether MOH could consider extending additional financial support for expectant mothers who find it difficult to obtain maternity insurance from private insurance companies due to previously-experienced pregnancy complications.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: MOH explained that this change is aimed at "full rider policies which encourage a 'buffer syndrome'" which leads to over-consumption, over-servicing and over-charging of healthcare services, which could, in turn, lead to higher fees and premiums over time.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I support this but it looks like most of the abuses comes from patients in private hospitals.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: From the numbers, it looks like there is a lower risk of overspending in the public hospitals.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The less financially savvy patients rely heavily on the hospital and their doctors to determine the course and cost of treatment.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This risk is further mitigated by the implementation of cost benchmarks in public hospitals.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In that light, will the Ministry consider having co-payment on IP riders only for private hospitals and have zero or lower co-payment for claims relating to public hospitals?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, one of the most effective ways to keep costs down is to provide transparency, thereby encouraging healthy competition among providers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Patients should have access to more information which include not only fees but also standard or quality of delivery.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Presently, fee benchmarks and bill amount information for common surgical procedures for both public and private hospitals are available on MOH's website.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope it is also possible for MOH to provide more qualitative information.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, besides providing more subsidies for more generic drugs, additional assistance for needy patients for drugs should also be well-understood by all public hospital staff so that they can advise patients accordingly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This issue was highlighted in the newspapers recently by members of the public.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It appeared that the affected patients and family members were not informed of the Medication Assistance Fund (MAF and MAF Plus), which is different from MediFund.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: MAF subsidises non-standard drugs prescribed for Pioneer Generation or CHAS cardholders.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Mr Chairman, a number of speakers before me have already raised most of the points which I have, so I will not repeat them and will be very brief.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: As Singapore's population ages, one of the issues which will be of increasing concern for our citizens is the affordability and accessibility of healthcare.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Given the importance and relevance of this issue for most Singaporeans, I am sure the Minister will provide some updates on what is being done or can be done to ensure that healthcare remains affordable for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: In particular, are there plans to use technology and medical advances to increase efficiencies, reduce doctors' time and empower other professionals within the healthcare ecosystem such that costs can be contained?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Could the Minister also clarify the extent to which generic drugs are used as another means of reducing costs?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: I believe Ms Joan Pereira has already raised this.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Could MOH also provide comfort to patients that generic drugs are just as efficacious as brand-name drugs?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Chairman, the Merdeka Generation Package (MGP) is a wide-ranging and comprehensive package of measures that addresses concerns that the Merdeka Generation (MG) would have regarding healthcare affordability.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: What are MOH's plans to reach out to the MG seniors to let them know about the MGP and support their aspirations for active ageing?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The total incentive of $4,000, together with the higher lifelong payouts, should be highlighted to the seniors during outreach activities, as they may be concerned about the higher monthly premiums.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: With longer lifespans, the risk of more seniors facing severe disability in their later years is higher.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: We can see for ourselves today, within our communities, many of the old-old, as we move from an aged society to a super-aged society, and with the old-old defined as those aged 85 and above, needing help with at least three out of six Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) of washing, dressing, feeding, transferring, toileting and walking.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: This proportion is growing higher day by day.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But that reform may take time to implement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: For now, I would like to ask how this appeals review process operates within MOH.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It would seem to be opaque to many in the profession.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What expertise and skillsets and processes are brought to bear in considering such appeals within MOH and what sorts of personnel are involved?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Next, once a complaint is escalated to an SMC Disciplinary Tribunal (DT), it is my understanding that lawyers begin to play a key role in the process.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Next, will the review process yield changes to reduce the long time period often associated with the CC and DT processes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And can the Government consider if disciplinary action for more minor complaints can be addressed by a different form of committee than a DT, to reduce the considerable time and cost associated with the DT process?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Lastly, the Government currently appoints the majority of members of the SMC.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What is the Government doing or will do to correct any perception now or in the future that the SMC is insufficiently independent of the Government?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If any such perception takes root, it may erode confidence among doctors of getting a fair hearing which, in turn, could lead to things like defensive medicine, which can escalate costs and worsen efficiency.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Mr Chairman, allied healthcare workers, such as nurses, physiotherapists and speech therapists, play a key role in supporting the overall medical care of the patient.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I had previously asked how we could formalise their continuing professional development, career progression and the sharing of best practices within the allied health profession.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Would MOH be able to provide an update on the steps taken so far to help achieve this outcome?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, demographics have only increased the demand for healthcare.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With more hospitals and polyclinics coming online in the communities to establish the key infrastructure for delivering healthcare needs to our people, it is time to look at the manpower available to operate and manage both the new and existing infrastructures.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A strong local core is important as healthcare needs are better served with cultural understanding.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even as we have learnt that the reduction in services Dependency Ratio Ceiling will not impact healthcare operations, how has this percentage shifted with the introduction of conversion programmes available at the tertiary institutions, such as the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT), and the push to increase intakes to the healthcare courses?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The retention rate of new healthcare workers will also be a key measure of sustainability of our healthcare operations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the attrition rate and average tenure of nurses and other healthcare workers?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the suite of measures to retain the local graduate healthcare workers in the industry sufficient?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And what are the common reasons for healthcare workers leaving the workforce?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Chairman, besides doctors and nurses, Allied Health Professionals and Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) practitioners make significant contributions to our healthcare ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: In a rapidly ageing country like ours, there will be greater demand for their services, particularly for therapists, psychologists, audiologists, dietitians and medical social workers, just to name a few.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: They are an integral part of a healthcare system which delivers comprehensive and seamless care.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: One, how is MOH ensuring that we will have a steady pipeline of Allied Health Professionals, given the need for holistic care?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Two, will there be measures to upskill and better empower nurses to take on a greater role in our healthcare system, given our tight labour market and the heavy work burdens of our nurses?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Three, in addition to the training and development of these professionals through the traditional career progression pathways, would the Ministry elaborate on measures to attract those interested in making a mid-career change to these professions?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Lastly, how would the Ministry ensure that the remunerations of those in the public sector remain competitive?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I have a few questions and suggestions for improving the intersection between the Government and VWOs in ILTC, though some of these points may apply to private sector developers and/or operators of ILTC facilities as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And this is not a bad thing as value-for-money is an important consideration.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Nevertheless, the ILTC sector is a space where innovation and experimentation are still relevant.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There should be space for facilities in our ILTC sector which are unorthodox, and which may come with a higher price tag, as it were.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What is the consideration given to striking the right balance between quality and innovation on the one hand and cost on the other?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Many lack the genuine understanding of what it is, and it also stems from the fact that it is a taboo subject many choose not to talk about and they feel discomfort in discussing it.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: It cuts across all ages because talking about death and the end of our lives are really not the easiest things.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: As a result, many lack the understanding and may be unaware of the important decisions and options they have or have to make whilst they still can.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: In my work as an Emergency Medicine Specialist, people come in with critical and serious illnesses and presentations, many even stemming from many years of harbouring a chronic illness or diagnosis, and yet, not having an Advance Care Planning (ACP) done at all.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: We then have to discuss with them or the next of kin at this critical juncture in order to have a decision to be made pertaining to the level and depth of care and resuscitation they wish.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Many grapple at this stage as they may not know what their loved ones wish for.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: They may never have broached the topic and a sense of guilt can prevail.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Choosing to know, learn and decide on ACP is really something we may need to do.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: How is the Ministry sending out more educational messaging and campaigns, perhaps to be executed in a sensitive way and also perhaps working across Ministries, such as MOH, the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) and other partnering organisations, VWOs and non-government organisations, and perhaps also getting our Inter-Religious Organisations and the Inter-Racial and Religious Confidence Circles to talk as well in our society.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to thank the Members for their thoughtful comments.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked for an update on our overall healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Global Burden of Disease 2017 Study published in The Lancet ranked Singapore favourably as the country with the highest life expectancy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But these figures also show that we are living about 10 years of our lives in ill health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For every 10 years we live, we spend more than a year in illness.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The mortality rates due to cancer, stroke and heart diseases have reduced significantly by 16%, from 2010 to 2017.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This was made possible in part due to the early prevention, better treatment and disease management, which have contributed to our increase in life expectancy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, it is not time for us to celebrate yet.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The recent Bloomberg report also reminds us that we need to keep up on our efforts.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Data also shows that many of us are living with chronic illness.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is partly due to an older population, but we cannot blame everything on an ageing population because it is also partly due to unhealthy lifestyles and habits.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If these chronic conditions are not managed well, more serious conditions may result further down the road.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: On capacity and accessibility, we have stepped up our building programmes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have completed seven hospitals since 2010 which will add up to about 3,800 number of beds when fully opened.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In 2018 itself, we opened the new Changi General Hospital Medical Centre, Sengkang General and Community Hospitals and, earlier this year, the new National University Centre for Oral Health Singapore commenced operations.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We also injected a significant supply of aged care services, especially in home and community care, to encourage ageing in place.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have been training and recruiting healthcare professionals to meet our manpower demand.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The number of registered doctors rose significantly, by 52% over the period from 2010 to 2018.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Local medicine intake increased by some 60%, from about 300 to about 500 today.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Together with Dentistry and Pharmacy, the total intake now exceeds 700 a year and contribute to a strong local pipeline, reducing our need for foreign-trained professionals.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Registered nurses have also increased significantly by 44%.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While we had a record local nursing intake of over 2,100 students last year, we will still need more, especially in the critical community care sector.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin will share more about opportunities for nursing and allied health professionals later.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have more than doubled the amount of direct Government subsidies given to Singaporeans from about $2.6 billion to $5.6 billion over the same period.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And this has helped to keep healthcare affordable, especially for needy Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, it is unsustainable for us to continue increasing our national healthcare expenditure at this current rate.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And I agree with Prof Fatimah Lateef that our healthcare system has to transform the way it delivers care and we must continue to refine our way of funding healthcare services.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As individuals, each of us must also take responsibility for our own health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our healthcare institutions are doing their part to transform their healthcare models.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Polyclinics, for example, have been experimenting with new ways to enhance chronic disease management.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The National Healthcare Group Polyclinics have piloted a teamlet care model since 2015.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: By assigning patients with chronic diseases to the same team comprising family physicians, nurse care managers as well as care coordinators, there is better continuity of care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As a result, patient outcomes have improved, with more regular preventive health screenings done, and visits to the doctors and emergency departments reduced.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: SingHealth Polyclinics and National University Polyclinics are also rolling out team-based care models.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Private GPs are our key partners in primary care, too.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Primary Care Network (PCN) started as a ground-up initiative by GPs from the Frontier Healthcare Group to share resources and improve chronic disease management.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Senior Minister of State Lam Pin Min will share more about the progress of the PCN scheme.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Similarly, we are working towards transforming care at the community level to better integrate social and healthcare services.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Community care providers are also doing their part.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some of them are piloting innovative ways to enhance patient care and safety.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, several of our community care providers, such as All Saints Home, have introduced new sensor mats to monitor residents’ movements so as to prevent falls and to provide better care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To catalyse efforts on care transformation, we set up the MOH Office for Healthcare Transformation (MOHT) in 2018.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: MOHT has been working with partners to design innovative healthcare pilots, such as the new Integrated General Hospital (IGH) model piloted at Alexandra Hospital (AH).

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This model particularly benefits patients with multiple active conditions, who would typically be attended to by a few specialists during each admission.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Under this new IGH model, one care team will look after each patient for better integrated care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Kang is an 81-year-old senior who lives alone and was recently admitted to AH for uncontrolled hypertension.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: He has a number of active medical conditions but was looked after by one care team, without transfers across wards and doctors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The care team found that Mr Kang's cataracts made it very difficult for him to take his medications and may increase future fall risks.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The team then reduced the pills he had to take and counselled him on how to take them properly.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: He also underwent cataract surgery and received physiotherapy, too.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: They also engaged community partners to schedule befriending and home care services, and connected Mr Kang to the Social Service Office (SSO) for post-discharge assistance and support.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: AH is now working to consolidate his outpatient care under one principal doctor.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu will be very happy to know that this pilot will be in Queenstown.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is still early days, and these efforts will need to be fully developed and evaluated before scaling up.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: MOH will continue our care transformation efforts, in line with our strategy to move Beyond Hospital to Community, Beyond Quality to Value, and Beyond Healthcare to Health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, there are a few key challenges ahead of us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First, we have to strengthen the robustness of our healthcare IT systems, including data privacy and security.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As highlighted by Mr de Souza, IT and data play an important role in our care transformation journey as they help to better inform policy, ensure continuity of care, and allow innovative care models to evolve.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The NEHR system, for example, is an important, large-scale national system designed to better support patient care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh and Ms Sylvia Lim asked about the safeguards in place for NEHR to ensure patient confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The first is the protection against cyberattacks and unauthorised access.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There are several lines of defences before the NEHR database, with intrusion detection at each line.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In addition, there are ongoing robustness tests conducted by the Cyber Security Agency (CSA), the Government Technology Agency and an independent third-party PricewaterhouseCoopers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the user level, the NEHR should only be used for direct patient care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There are strict controls to protect against unauthorised access.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The NEHR system also does not allow users to download records onto workstations.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As highlighted by Mr Christopher de Souza, having well-trained IT and cybersecurity specialists familiar with healthcare is key.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: MOH, with CSA’s support, is working to ensure that technical training for our cybersecurity specialists meets the industry's best practices and standards.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Good cyber hygiene practices are regularly shared with all public healthcare staff.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we must assume that persistent attackers will not give up and they will eventually get through, despite the strongest protection.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, the second level of safeguards is having proper detection and enforcement measures to pick up any breaches quickly and escalate to the appropriate level for prompt investigation and containment.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Integrated Health Information System plans to roll out a feature that will allow patients to view accesses made to their NEHR records so that they, too, can report any suspicious access.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We must take stern action against anyone who is responsible for data breaches, including our staff who have failed in their duties.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This way, we can ensure a strong data protection system.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As Mr Charles Chong pointed out, all stakeholders must work together to ensure that our healthcare system will be sustainable not just for our current needs but also for the needs of our future generations.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The MGP is our way of honouring the MG for their unique contributions in shaping the nation during our formative years.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Package is designed to support MG seniors in leading a healthy and active life as they age, and to provide assurance that they will be able to afford their care expenses.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor will share more details on MGP later.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong will update on our proposed enhancements to CHAS so that all Singaporeans will have access to affordable quality primary care, especially for their chronic conditions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Healthcare providers and professionals, too, play an important role in keeping healthcare costs in check, through ensuring efficient operations and abiding by appropriate pricing and clinical practices.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We had introduced fee benchmarks last year to provide all stakeholders with a useful reference on appropriate fee levels.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have also studied best practices and approaches on value-based healthcare in the US and elsewhere, which Mr Leon Perera asked about, and adapted it to our local context.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is also difficult for me to explain value-based healthcare in two minutes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: More work will need to be done and we are continuing to explore this.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Insurance allows risks and resources to be shared across all members in the pool, helping patients to cope with large and unexpected healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is why we have MediShield Life and, soon, CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will continue to explore how we can further strengthen the role of insurance as we move forward.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Lastly, individuals have the responsibility of saving for our own healthcare needs during our working years, including through MediSave, to meet our future needs when we grow old.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We also have the responsibility to make well-informed decisions to choose appropriate healthcare services.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But the most effective way to keep healthcare affordable is to stay healthy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The next challenge is, therefore, to take more decisive steps to encourage healthy living.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Three years ago, I declared war on diabetes in this House.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is probably the only war that the Parliament has ever declared.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have made some progress but we do need to push harder.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We held a Ministerial Conference on Diabetes last year and one of the key takeaways is that to tackle diabetes effectively, we need a coordinated effort by all stakeholders, not just MOH.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: My colleagues will elaborate more on these efforts later.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Smoking is another area that we need to move more swiftly and strategically on.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Tobacco use is the second-highest contributor to Singapore’s disease burden.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will continue to work on reducing smoking rates.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, despite our best efforts to stay healthy, we may still fall ill and become frail as we age.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Caregivers will need greater support as they will play a key role in caring for the sick and frail among us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: With an ageing population and longer life expectancy, caregiving needs will rise, with family and informal caregivers playing an increasingly important role.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Many will have to balance their work and family responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There is, therefore, greater urgency for the society to come together and collectively support our caregivers and ensure that adequate "hardware" and "heartware" are in place.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: (In Mandarin):   	Mr Tang, who is 42 years old, heads the business development department of his company.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In the past year or so, Mr Tang has been caring for his 81-year-old father with dementia, together with his mother, wife and siblings.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While his mother is the main caregiver, the other family members also take turns to help care for his father.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Although Mr Tang and his family faced challenges adapting to his father's behavioural changes, it was fortunate that his wife works in the healthcare sector, and the family was able to identify various avenues of support and help.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Nonetheless, not all caregivers are equipped with such knowledge, or have other family members to share the caregiving burden.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: With our ageing population, caregiving needs will grow and we need to strengthen the support for our caregivers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We need to increase awareness of the resources that are available to caregivers, and more systematically match these caregivers to the help they require.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: (In English): I have spoken about our progress, transformative initiatives that can change our care models, and MOH's focus areas for the next three to five years.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But at the heart of our healthcare strategies is people – people like you and I.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: MOH and our healthcare providers can only do so much.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For every "top-down" programme, we need many "ground-up" support and initiatives.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Each of us must actively take charge of our health and come together as a community, or just as a group of friends, to support one another.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is why I find the example of "Team Strong Silvers" so inspiring.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is a group of friends with a common interest in health and fitness who decided to form a senior citizens’ interest group in 2013.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Just like its name suggests, the members build up their strength through calisthenic exercises.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The team hopes to encourage more seniors to age actively, and to inspire younger generations to invest in their health from an earlier age.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I am glad to see the team actively spreading the healthy lifestyle message via social media and even carrying out onsite fitness training sessions for other seniors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: With more seniors like them, I am hopeful that we will add more years of healthy life to our growing life expectancy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And when we replace "I" with "We" and do it together, "Illness" can become "Wellness".

speaker: The Chairman
text: Every Wednesday, we will have Parliament running in the evenings.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Are we building enough infrastructure, such as acute hospitals, community hospitals, nursing homes, dementia-care, palliative-care and respite homes and so on?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Can we also provide more daycare centres, dementia, rehabilitation and respite daycare centres, and senior activity centres (SACs)?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Are we training enough medical personnel to cushion the impending explosion on the need for healthcare providers?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Last year, the social aged care functions, under the Senior Cluster Network, was transferred from MSF to MOH.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: What are MOH's plans to better support an ageing population with its expanded functions?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: One important form of preventive healthcare is allowing seniors to remain active and independent within the community and living in their own homes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is because being active and independent in the community will facilitate the physical, mental and social well-being of seniors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: As what the Finance Minister said, "The best way of protecting ourselves is to lead a healthy lifestyle".

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: What is MOH doing to support seniors who wish to remain independent in the community?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many seniors have expressed that they prefer to live for as long as possible in their own homes, in the familiar environment and in the community with families and friends.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We should also encourage the community to come together to make this work.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Every few HDB blocks should have at least one SAC to promote the physical, mental and social wellness of the mobile seniors and to facilitate them to remain active and healthy in the community.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: VWOs can be roped in to provide the assistance to the seniors to fill the gaps.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to expand homecare expeditiously to allow seniors with medical conditions to remain in their own homes and in the community.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is especially useful after discharge from hospitals.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Under homecare, MOH can facilitate services, such as medical caregiving, nursing, medication, nutrition, occupational and rehabilitation therapy.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Physiotherapy at home is especially crucial to allow earlier regaining of mobility from reversible medical conditions, such as mild strokes and surgeries.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: At discharge from hospitals, patients can be dispensed with mobility aids to facilitate independent living at home.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Homecare aides can be recruited and trained to provide specific job scopes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Transitional Care Programme by acute hospitals to help caregivers look after their loved ones at home enhances homecare and should be expanded.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Seniors with ADL deficiency need caregivers for their daily living.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many caregivers are family members who also hold employment.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could our Government facilitate flexible work arrangements (FWAs) for caregivers?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Would our Government also consider paid "Care Leave" for caregivers?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It can be two weeks per year, for a start, similar to "Parental Leave" for fathers.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Caregivers can suffer "burnout syndrome" from emotional and physical fatigue.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could we have more respite care centres that are accessible and affordable?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could there be a one-stop centre for information and respite care referrals for caregivers?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many caregivers also get domestic helpers to assist them with their caregiving roles.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: However, many foreign domestic helpers are ill-equipped to take up this role.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could we improve the know-how and enforce this area of domestic employment requirement?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could we provide more housing adaptability to accommodate seniors' mobility to facilitate independent living, as well as having a seniors-friendly environment in the vicinity, such as food centres, health facility and wellness centres?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Examples of housing adaptability are doors for motorised mobility aids, appropriate-height kitchen tabletops, hoisting aids to get out of bed, emergency call points and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Technology adaptability, such as smart home aids for seniors, fall sensors, emergency medical detection sensors, can enhance quality of life.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: I would also like to take this opportunity to share some suggestions which I hope can be considered for SACs’ future development.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: As a communal space for social and recreational activities, the number and capacity of the programmes must be able to cope with the higher demand which will come with more seniors taking up active ageing.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Second, I hope all SACs will have sufficient attached daycare, respite care and assisted living facilities to provide a seamless experience for the elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Imagine a healthy, active senior who has taken part in the SAC's activities transiting into its respite and daycare services, and subsequently assisted living facilities, as he grows older and more frail.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: The proximity of all these to his home, the familiarity of the environment, staff, neighbours, fellow participants and volunteers will provide him or her with a lot of comfort and peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the additional funding from the Long-Term Care Support Fund and Home Caregiving Grant is likely to boost the use of formal home- and centre-based services.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There is a need, therefore, to improve the regulatory framework for homecare and daycare services.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps it is time to consolidate existing healthcare legislation into a holistic framework that covers the whole care spectrum.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A strong regulatory framework should have at least three components: legislation, care quality auditing, and feedback and disputes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Independent bodies and a rating system could be set up for these purposes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: As we enhance our healthcare, we can expect longer and more healthy years.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Future work will also rely more on intellect and wisdom.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Our population will become better educated and more savvy with the digital space and, therefore, less fear and deeper entrenchment of technology in our lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: There is, therefore, much that we can do to help seniors age meaningfully.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: More importantly, we need to ensure that our seniors do not slip into isolation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We need to ensure that they are constantly connected to our larger social network.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I had spoken many times in this House about how to enable active aging and what seniors can do.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I would also like to highlight one point today and, that is, lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: It is exciting to explore new things and exhilarating to achieve what we did not know or have before.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We should re-ignite that sense of curiosity in our seniors and offer many opportunities for them to learn new things.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: SkillsFuture is an excellent scheme to promote lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: The National Silver Academy also offers a variety of courses tailored for seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Some of the seniors in MacPherson have actively utilised the credits and attend courses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: That is why we launched the Lifelong Learning Fund in MacPherson, so that they can continue to take on courses and acquire new knowledge and skills, especially in the digital space.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: What plan does the Ministry have to encourage more seniors to embrace lifelong learning?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It may be timely to review our "investment" in health over the years and determine how we have fared thus far and what targets we should aim for the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: My attention was recently drawn to a study published earlier this year in the Singapore Medical Journal by a group of 10 doctors and researchers entitled "Successful ageing in Singapore".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The study focused on successful ageing amongst Singaporeans aged 60 and older.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Successful ageing is defined as having no major diseases, no disability, high cognitive functions as well as physical functions and active life engagement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: What is the Minister's view of the finding in light of the "investments" made in promoting good health over the years and against the backdrop of an increase in lifestyle diseases, as the hon Minister just mentioned?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: This requires putting in place home and community care support, programmes to engage and promote active ageing, infrastructural investments, retrofitting and hardware maintenance to create an elderly-friendly environment where seniors can live independently.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We should apply elder-friendly designs into our hardware and heartware solutions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Share best practices and set standards and audit public and private projects across all sectors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We should proliferate digital eldercare to supplement the shortage of manpower.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Leverage technology and artificial intelligence to enable quality and personalised care for seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Continue to research, develop and invest in digital eldercare solutions so that more innovations can reach the market faster.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We could do more to recruit and organise volunteers into a powerful network of resources in the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Exploit physical and digital platforms to optimise the matching of regular and ad hoc volunteers to help seniors who may have differing needs at different times of the day.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: In essence, we can still do more to enable independent living for seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I would, therefore, like to ask what is the Ministry and the whole of Government doing to help seniors live independently.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: What is being done in terms of physical hardware and programmes?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How is the Government actively utilising digital solutions to achieve our goals?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Caregivers play a very important role in our ageing landscape.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: They offer the human touch that Government policies or programmes cannot provide, no matter how brilliantly designed they can be.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Not all caregivers who are still working can successfully negotiate for FWAs or, at least, not as easily, depending on the employer's attitude and the nature of the job.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Even as the night respite care pilot is underway, there is still an army of caregivers embedded in different parts of our community providing non-stop care to their loved ones and quietly enduring the inevitable fatigue.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Mr Chairman, one result of us having an ageing population is that more support will need to be given to elderly Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Apart from those who care for the elderly, there are also those who care for people with disabilities, for those with chronic or terminal illnesses.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Very often, these caregivers are family members – children, parents or siblings.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: The demands placed on caregivers must not be underestimated.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Apart from the stresses involved with looking after persons under their care, they also have their own lives to lead.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: And while I believe that most caregivers embrace the caring responsibilities, they often face their own challenges, and these could be professional, financial or psychological.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Caregivers play a vital role in ensuring the well-being of our older citizens and citizens with disabilities or chronic illnesses.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: And it is only right if we do what we can to support them.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Could the Minister also consider, if beyond the existing schemes, the financial needs of caregivers, something that we can look into supporting, as being part of the broader package of support for the person who is receiving the care?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is not unusual for such patients not to adhere to instructions to take their medication or even attend medical appointments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
