text: This would lead to relapses on the part of the patients.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Often, their caregivers undergo quite a bit of stress as a result.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There are also families where the caregivers are older than the patients, giving rise to uncertainty and worry on the part of caregivers as to how the patients, usually their children, would be taken care of once they pass on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong pertinently recognised in his speech at the debate that there is a "broad range of caregivers who operate in a variety of different circumstances and a very broad landscape".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is time to consider providing similar support for caregivers of mental health patients as that announced for the caregivers of seniors.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Separately, there are a good number of cases of mental health patients who live alone or do not get any support from family members and are in sore need of medical intervention.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: From time to time, we hear of such patients engaged in behaviour, such as hoarding materials in common corridors of HDB flats, quarrelling with neighbours based on perceived threats, throwing bags of urine and faeces and so on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: A good number of them cannot help themselves because they suffer from anti-social personality disorders whose prognosis is guarded.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Often, in the absence of supervision from families, there are practical difficulties in ensuring that these patients receive and adhere to their treatment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Even if the Police get called in, and the patients are eventually referred to the Institute of Mental Health (IMH), there is no guarantee that they would present themselves at scheduled appointments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Once they are off their medicine, the tendency is for them to go back to their anti-social behaviour and the entire cycle repeats itself.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This raises a conundrum in the communities where they live.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Not only that, these patients may harm themselves, especially if they plunge into depression.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Also, how can the community and other partners help in this regard?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chairman, there is an increasing need to ensure that we make mental health services more accessible to support those with mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A distinction is often made between mental and physical health.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But the mind and body are inextricably linked.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The two are inseparable and we need to pay attention to both to achieve wellness and not fall into illness.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our workplace can be a very stressful environment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Prolonged exposure to such stress can potentially lead to mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But there remains a societal stigma when it comes to dealing with mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mental health issues affect Singaporeans of all ages, in particular, our youths and millennials.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some have started calling them the "burnout generation".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Yet, addressing such issues remain a stigma in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Mr Chairman, staying engaged, being active and socialising are key to good mental health.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If one has physical health but is not connected to a social network, then mental health can decline.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is one of the reasons why we have situated a childcare centre next to an active ageing centre in the constituency I serve in Ulu Pandan.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The elderly and young can interact and bring joy to each other, across generations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As an extra step, would MOH consider setting up Community Mental Wellness Conservatories in heartland areas to bring together caregivers of elderly Singaporeans who may have dementia or mental illnesses to share caregiving best practices on how to reconnect the elderly to a social network, with the mind to lift their spirits and re-energise them into joyful and active ageing?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have made the same request consistently since then.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As early as in 1991, the viability limit defined in the Motherhood Protection Act in Japan was amended from 24 weeks to 22 weeks based on medical advances.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am certain that if we look at the numbers in our own hospitals, there will be similar medical justifications.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Mandarin, Japanese and Korean, the written word for the womb translates to "the palace of the child".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Hebrew, the word Rakh'am is used to refer to the womb and translates to compassion and protection from harm.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Women are living longer and have longer life expectancy than men.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Women are also typically the main caregiver at home, caring for our young and old.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Their health, therefore, not only concern herself but will impact the entire family's well-being.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Moreover, women is a formidable source of manpower for Singapore, driving our continued growth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: It is, therefore, important that we ensure Singaporean women are healthy and vibrant.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I would thus like to ask what the Ministry is doing to help women and mothers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: What is in place to drive preventive health effort for women?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This House recently saw a lively debate on ageing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I was encouraged by the support for the Action Plan for Successful Ageing launched in 2015, when I shared about its progress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As Minister Gan Kim Yong shared, our Life Expectancy and Healthy Life Expectancy are good.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Nonetheless, through the Action Plan, we want to further help Singaporeans add more life to years, not just years to life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As we provide for seniors today, we will do more for seniors of tomorrow, who will live longer, be better educated and have different aspirations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: A study by the Duke-National University of Singapore (NUS) Centre for Ageing Research and Education showed that seniors who are supported by social networks and befriending can better manage their chronic diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Strengthening integration between social and healthcare is key to successful ageing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: First, we want to further enable people in the social and health sectors to integrate care for our seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Seniors can have their social and healthcare needs managed jointly by the Silver Generation Office (SGO) and Social Service Offices (SSOs).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: More of these offices will be co-located where possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: SGO is recruiting more SGAs to reach out to seniors, including the MG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I encourage Singaporeans to come forward and join this endeavour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: MOH works closely with our community care providers and healthcare professionals to deliver quality care, ensuring good governance over our services, while allowing room for the sector to evolve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To Ms Anthea Ong's query, in 2015, MOH developed developmental guidelines for home and daycare providers to work towards quality care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Healthcare professionals providing these services, such as doctors, nurses and therapists, must also be licensed by their professional bodies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Second, we will strengthen integration by providing places and programmes to address the social and healthcare needs of our seniors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In response to Ms Joan Pereira and Dr Lily Neo, we aspire towards more age-friendly neighbourhoods, with accessible care and amenities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are expanding aged care services capacity but must do so sustainably.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will partner our operators to enhance the scope and reach of services in our Senior Centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, those currently providing daycare services may offer additional wellness programmes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Services will be made available to all seniors, not just those living in studio apartments and rental flats.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will work with operators, enhancing their capacity and capabilities, to implement this common vision of SACs, SCCs and AAHs as places where seniors can access a range of services from fiscal year 2020.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In relation to Mr Leon Perera's question, since 2012, we introduced the Build-Own-Lease framework to support efforts to increase capacity, encourage improvements in care quality while keeping fees affordable.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our tender process covers quality, including innovative care models, and affordable fees.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) supports providers in capability development, including leadership development, manpower recruitment and quality improvement programmes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Members, such as Ms Rahayu Mahzam, have called for Assisted Living options.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For instance, healthy seniors could buy into basic services, such as light housekeeping.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Additional services, like care coordination, can be layered on as their needs change.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have identified a possible location, and MND will share more on this.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The development could comprise flats with senior-friendly features, complemented by communal spaces like recreation-cum-dining rooms with light programming to encourage interaction.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH and MND will start Focus Group Discussions over the next few months to better understand Singaporeans' aspirations and finetune this new option for ageing-in-place before going to market.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As Ms Tin Pei Ling suggested, we are tapping on technology to benefit seniors, starting with MG seniors who are more IT-literate.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH is partnering the Smart Nation and Digital Government Office and the Public Service Division to include a new module under the existing Moments of Life app to support active ageing.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I have seen a prototype and found it useful.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The app will include an Active Ageing Programme finder that can show seniors programmes near their homes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Seniors can also use the app to check their eligibility for Government benefits like the MGP and the Goods and Services Tax Voucher scheme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In a later phase, we will explore features, such as allowing bookings for active ageing programmes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The app will be piloted later this year, and I look forward to using and sharing it.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: An ageing population raises demand for community mental health services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Someone once jokingly said to me, "The nice thing about ageing and losing your memory is that you make new friends every day!" Jokes aside, in reality, dementia can be debilitating not just to patients but also caregivers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I agree with Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Melvin Yong as well as Ms Anthea Ong that we must support persons with mental health conditions and their caregivers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In 2017, arising from the recommendations of the Inter-agency Committee on Community Mental Health, MOH launched the enhanced Community Mental Health Masterplan to further strengthen mental healthcare.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have made good progress since in increasing outreach, early detection and providing care and support in the community.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Through a multi-pronged approach strategy, we bring the community together to raise awareness and support for seniors with or are at-risk of dementia and depression.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are on track to meet our 2021 target of 50 teams.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We established eight Dementia-Friendly Communities, building networks of support around those with dementia and their caregivers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our Community Network for Seniors (CNS) has been expanded nationwide to anchor a strong community care system for seniors, including those with mental health conditions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Under CNS, SGAs proactively reach out to seniors, referring those with possible mental health conditions to support services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Community befrienders visit lonely seniors regularly, providing them with emotional support to keep social isolation and depression at bay.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Furthermore, AIC has trained over 14,000 frontline staff from Government agencies and community partners to identify and respond to persons with mental health conditions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Over 2,700 individuals have been supported with medical care or social support according to their needs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to work with agencies like the Ministry of Home Affairs and HDB, grassroots leaders and VWOs to identify and provide social and medical support for those in need, including persons who exhibit behavioural challenges in the community.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Addressing the stigma associated with mental health conditions is also a collective effort.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NCSS and IMH launched the "Beyond the Label" campaign in September 2018.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We hope this will catalyse more conversations about mental health and encourage those facing such challenges to seek help.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Twenty allied health-led community intervention teams were established to support GPs and community organisations in managing persons with mental health conditions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Beyond building on existing efforts and scaling up programmes, we are developing new initiatives to better address emerging areas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Following the NurtureSG Taskforce's recommendation to better support youths, the Ministry of Education (MOE) and HPB have been establishing peer support structures in mainstream schools and Institutes of Higher Learning to equip students to look out for signs of mental stress among peers, and support and encourage them to seek help when needed.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Since 2007, about 2,400 Allied Educators have received training to identify and support students who require referrals to mental health services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Community Health Assessment Team (CHAT) operates a mental health wellness centre for youths, which has reached out and provided mental health assessment to more than 3,100 at-risk youths as of December last year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As social and mental health issues are interlinked, we will take a more holistic approach for at-risk youths.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will develop a new integrated youth service, together with community youth partners, IMH, AIC, NCSS and HPB.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will expand on the success of the CHAT model to increase outreach and educate youths on resilience and mental well-being.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Those who need help will be referred to social and health services for assistance and intervention in an integrated manner.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will update the enhanced Community Mental Health Masterplan and rally a whole-of-society effort to build communities of care around mental health patients and their caregivers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MGP is a major fiscal undertaking and is our show of appreciation and support for the MG in their silver years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: After the Prime Minister announced the MGP at the National Day Rally last year, many of my MG cohort friends excitedly asked me "What, what, what are the benefits?" Following Minister Heng Swee Keat's Budget speech, the constant refrain became "When, when, when, when will I get these benefits?" We want our MG seniors to benefit from the package as soon as possible.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Implementing the MGP is a major effort involving multiple Government agencies and partners, and we are working closely to roll out the benefits quickly.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: From July 2019, MG seniors will receive three benefits.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Two, additional MediShield Life premium subsidies for MG seniors will take effect.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MG seniors will receive subsidies starting from 5% of their MediShield Life annual premiums and increasing to 10% after reaching 75 years old.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Although system changes to automatically apply the additional subsidies will be ready only towards the end of this year, we will backdate the subsidies to 1 July, to allow more MG seniors to enjoy them.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MG seniors with policy renewals between 1 July and 31 October this year will pay the full premium first and receive the additional subsidies as a refund automatically by the end December 2019.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Three, the one-time $100 top-up to their PAssion Silver cards, we will share more details on how to redeem the top-up when ready.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As they will have till 31 December next year to do so, and the credits do not expire, we would like to assure all our MG seniors that there is no need to rush.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Come 1 November 2019, MG seniors will receive additional subsidies for outpatient care, for life.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Implementing the outpatient subsidies involves many healthcare partners, who need to train frontline staff and make necessary system changes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We need time to do this properly and correctly so that implementation can be as smooth as possible.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MG seniors can also bring their MG cards when they visit CHAS GP and dental clinics, to enjoy special subsidies of up to $23.50 per visit for common illnesses, $520 in annual chronic subsidies and $261.50 per procedure for dental procedures.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Also, eligible MG seniors will pay only $2 for screenings recommended under the Screen for Life programme, compared to up to $5 today.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MG seniors who join CareShield Life will hence receive participation incentives totalling $4,000 each, which will offset annual premiums for 10 years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Eligible seniors will receive a notification letter for the MGP by April 2019.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: From the same month, SGO will start to proactively reach out to 500,000 MG seniors to share details of the MGP.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To Dr Chia Shi-Lu's query, beyond home visits, SGO will employ new approaches, such as group engagements at workplaces, which may be preferred by MG seniors, among whom one in two are working.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: SGO will also conduct engagements at community locations frequented by MG seniors, like hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It will connect MG seniors to volunteering and learning opportunities, such as the Retire with a Purpose (RWAP) programme under the Organisation of Senior Volunteers (RSVP) and National Silver Academy courses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As mentioned by Minister Gan Kim Yong, Senior Minister of State Sim Ann and I will co-chair an MG Communications and Engagement Taskforce to ensure effective communications and outreach to our MGs and their family members.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The taskforce comprises 23 members from the public, private and people sectors, which had its first meeting two weeks ago.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling noted that women are living longer and we must address their healthcare needs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Women's Health Committee will continue to champion good health among Singaporean women at all stages of their life.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: From 2011 to 2015, about 200 new cases were diagnosed annually and around 70 die of the disease every year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This cancer, which is caused by infection with the Human Papilloma Virus (HPV), can be prevented with vaccination and screening.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: All other female Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents (PRs) from the same age-equivalent cohorts, including those studying in private education institutions, will also be eligible.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The vaccination will be fully subsidised, as part of an opt-in scheme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The better test will cost more, but the Government will provide more subsidies, so the cost to women will be the same in the long run.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will also make early screening more convenient for women with an history of gestational diabetes, who are at higher risk of diabetes later in life and need to start regular screening soon after pregnancy.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They will be automatically eligible for subsidised cardiovascular risk screening under the Screen for Life programme, and will no longer need to take the online diabetes risk assessment tool to qualify.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is because MediShield Life and MediSave now provide basic healthcare coverage for all Singaporeans from birth.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Dennis Tan asked about attracting more Singaporeans to nursing and supporting continuing development and career progression of healthcare professionals.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Over the last five years, we increased nursing intakes by around 30%.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In 2018, we admitted more than 2,100 students, our highest intake to date, up from 1,600 in 2013.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But it will be challenging to continually increase student intakes in view of falling cohort sizes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, we need to look at mid-careerists, too, beyond supplementing our local workforce with foreigners.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For those looking for a second career in healthcare, our Professional Conversion Programmes (PCPs) provide sponsorship for course fees and an allowance.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In 2018, about 130 mid-career individuals embarked on our nursing PCPs, our highest intake in 10 years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will continue to work with healthcare employers to improve retention, provide meaningful job opportunities, and enhance careers through multiple progression pathways and entry points to ensure we maintain a strong local core of the nursing workforce.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In line with the SkillsFuture movement, we worked with Nanyang and Ngee Ann Polytechnics to create a new, faster progression pathway for Enrolled Nurses who did well during their Institute of Technical Education (ITE) training, to upskill to a Registered Nurse.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We now have a 2+2 Diploma in Nursing which will allow ITE upgraders to complete the Diploma in Nursing course in two years instead of the current 2.5 years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will strengthen and better recognise workplace-based learning, to achieve the twin objectives of better care for our patients and professional growth for our healthcare staff.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NNA will oversee Continuing Education and Training efforts to develop future-ready nurses with the requisite skills and competencies to meet evolving healthcare needs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In line with the push towards digitalisation, the NNA platform will allow nurses and healthcare leaders to access a comprehensive suite of high-quality courses and learning opportunities online.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Today, many healthcare providers have inhouse training programmes which are often not recognised and transferable across different institutions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Chairman, in conclusion, as MOH continues to empower all Singaporeans to take charge of our health, I invite everyone to work with us to add more life to years.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.02 pm until 3.25 pm.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Thus, I agree with the Minister for Finance wholeheartedly when he said, "The best way of protecting ourselves is to lead a healthy lifestyle and take preventive actions".

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This is the best approach as it will result in quality of life and a happier populace.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Preventive healthcare means adopting healthy lifestyles to stay healthy and to prevent diseases, especially chronic diseases.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: It also means detecting and treating chronic diseases early and consistently.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The purpose is to prevent severe ill health and disability as a result of chronic diseases like diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Untreated, chronic diseases can lead to heart diseases, stroke, renal failure, foot amputation, blindness and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: We cannot carry on with just the traditional approach of healthcare systems on diagnosing and treating diseases alone, because this will lead to increasing demand on healthcare services, which can be daunting in an ageing population.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This will encourage more people to seek treatment early for chronic diseases.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Subsidising the treatment for chronic diseases is a good way to prevent the complications of such diseases, will reduce ill health and lessen the demand for acute care.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: It will be a pity if we have such a good CHAS scheme but people do not make full use of it.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This may be due to either insufficient information about the scheme or the patients are not bothered to go for early and continuous treatment of chronic diseases, due to a lack of knowledge of chronic diseases and their side effects.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I urge MOH to raise awareness and campaign on the importance of early diagnosis and treatment of chronic diseases.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Could MOH provide an update on the war on diabetes, the Healthy SG task force and HPB’s progress on healthy lifestyle promotion?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Promotion of mental well-being is an integral part of preventive healthcare.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Presently, MOH's psychiatric and mental healthcare is insufficient, especially in the community setting.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Could MOH expand and provide more resources in this area?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: There is a saying "We are what we eat".

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: However, Singaporeans are already taking more than twice that.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Excessive sugar intake may result in excessive weight, diabetes, heart diseases, fatty liver and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Could MOH strategise more effectively to nudge Singaporeans to reduce their sugar intake?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: MOH will need to adopt a range of measures, including better information and a national campaign to facilitate better-informed choices.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Labelling of the sugar and calorie contents should be made widely available in the food on sale here, even at our hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Such information will not only remind people to keep healthy but also give consumers an informed choice, to better plan their sugar and calorie intake for the day.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I favour to go for "half of your sugar intake or no sugar intake" campaign.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Other measures should include sugar taxation and to reduce the sugar content in beverages.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: In our schools, we can go further in helping our children by reducing their palate for sweetness, by not selling beverages and other sugar-added food in school canteens.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: We should facilitate our young to achieve a reduced palate for sweetness when they are in schools, so as to achieve better health when they grow up.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Mr Chairman, during the 2017 National Day Rally, Prime Minister Lee cited Diabetes as a health crisis for Malays and Indians.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: He pointed out that the main common causes of death like stroke, heart attack and kidney failure can be traced back to diabetes.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Can the Minister share what efforts are undertaken to customise health promotional messages to the Malay and Indian communities?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Could the Minister also provide an update on the war on diabetes?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Mr Chairman, it has been quite a few years since MOH declared war on diabetes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Singaporeans spend a lot of time at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Therefore, promoting workplace health is a key battleground in our fight against diabetes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: We are what we eat, meals with reduced salt and oil, and drinks with reduced sugar are some simple steps that workers can take towards forming healthy eating habits.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Employers, too, can play a vital role in encourage healthier eating habits.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: The National Transport Workers Union (NTWU) and Singapore Bus Services Transit (SBST) have collaborated to do just that.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: More than 10,000 SBST staff can get a stamp with each brown rice meal they buy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Every five stamps can be exchanged for a $2.50 meal voucher.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Since we started this initiative, our transport workers have taken more than 50,000 brown rice meals at our NTWU canteens.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: I hope that MOH can continue to encourage and support more such collaborations at our workplaces.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Such products are particularly appealing to new smokers, especially youths.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: WHO has also recently introduced the concept of a "best buy" policy.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: How aligned is Singapore with WHO's recommended, cost-effective policy action for smoking?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Can more be done to help smokers, particularly young ones?

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Chairman, with our high life expectancy, we are facing an increasing burden of chronic diseases, coupled with rising healthcare costs and emerging diseases.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We need to be ready to meet these challenges.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I will share more on the work we have done to keep Singaporeans healthy and safe, while keeping healthcare affordable for all.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Primary care plays a crucial role as the foundation of our healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It enables good quality, comprehensive and continued care for Singaporeans near their homes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to invest in our primary care to enhance facilities, and provide more resources for our GP partners.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Minister Gan earlier shared about our primary care transformation efforts, including the PCN scheme, of which Dr Chia Shi-Lu has asked for an update.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Please allow me to share more in Mandarin.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: (In Mandarin):   In 2018, MOH launched the PCN scheme.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is part of our strategy to transform primary care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This scheme aims to support private GPs to come together to form networks with the sharing of clinical and administrative resources, and provide more holistic care for patients with chronic diseases.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Through this scheme, patients with diabetes have enhanced accessibility to various ancillary services, such as eye and foot checks.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This number is more than 40% of CHAS GP clinics.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: (In English): Mr Chairman, let me now share a success story from United PCN.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Like many Singaporeans, Mr Adrian Chia, who is 38 years old, loves food.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: He used to drink a 1.5-litre bottle of sweetened beverage daily, and ate fried and oily food.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: He was diagnosed with diabetes by his GP, Dr Kelvin Goh, who practices in a clinic under United PCN.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Chia took his diagnosis as a wake-up call.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Working together with Dr Goh, the PCN nurse and care coordinator supported Mr Chia with managing his condition.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: He also received nurse counselling for his diabetes, as well as foot and eye screening checks through the PCN.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Chia began to take small steps, and started to exercise daily.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Through much perseverance and self-motivation, he has progressed to participating in Iron Man races.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: He also changed his eating habits to include healthier food choices, such as oatmeal and fruits.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Today, Mr Chia's condition is now under control, and may not even require diabetes medicine if he maintains his new regime.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu has also asked about our efforts to support PCN clinics in tracking and monitoring patients' progress.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: A key feature of the PCN scheme is the provision of resources to maintain a chronic disease registry that tracks the care processes and patient outcomes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: By aggregating resources through PCN networks, GPs in the PCN scheme also stand to benefit from greater economies of scale.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, NUHS PCN in the Western region has worked with major laboratory providers to provide common laboratory tests for chronic disease management at reduced prices, and facilitate the electronic collation of laboratory results for the chronic disease registry, reducing the need for GPs to manually compile these.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Such systematic data collection allows PCN GPs to reflect on their professional practice and work with the PCN headquarters to implement quality improvement programmes and improve patient outcomes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Learning from the experience of PCNs, MOH will study how to help CHAS clinics better track their patients’ progress and outcomes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH will also continue to encourage more GPs to join CHAS, though there are always some who chose not to, such as those who prefer not to take on additional loads.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the same time, we have continued our efforts in the War on Diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Mohamed Irshad have asked for an update on this.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We should recognise that our fellow Singaporeans with diabetes do not have to journey alone; we all play a part in supporting them to better manage their condition, and avoid long-term complications from diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Patient empowerment has emerged as a new paradigm that can help improve medical outcomes while lowering costs of treatment.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This concept seems particularly promising in the management of chronic diseases, including diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As such, the Diabetes Prevention and Care Taskforce has developed a new Patient Empowerment for Self-Care Framework which aims to empower patients to co-own their care journeys for better care outcomes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It helps patients initiate and sustain lifestyle changes for better disease management, prioritising what is of greatest importance to them.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is done with the support of their families, healthcare professionals, community-based providers, as well as other forms of social support.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have developed the national diabetes reference materials for patients, caregivers and the public.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The first tranche of materials is largely pictorial and easy to understand.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will also be seeking public views from mid-2019 on specific diabetes-related topics for more in-depth materials to be developed and published online for reference.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Besides empowering our patients, our healthcare workers can look forward to more training and resources to improve their delivery of care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH will be developing a care team training framework to equip healthcare professionals, and lay volunteers in the community, with essential skills to empower their patients and caregivers more effectively.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This will be developed in consultation with various stakeholders and rolled out progressively from end-2019.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Last year, I shared about our high rate of diabetes-related amputations of the leg and foot.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH will continue to closely track the rate of amputations among patients with diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Aside from equipping our healthcare professionals, MOH also seeks to uphold the standards of practice and public confidence in the medical profession.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The medical disciplinary process is specified in the Medical Registration Act (MRA) and aims to protect both the public and ensure fairness to the doctors.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Leon Perera has given some feedback and asked about the review of the medical disciplinary process.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH is currently looking into making amendments to the MRA, which was last amended in 2010.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This will include looking at the issues raised by Mr Leon Perera.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In addition, as announced over the weekend, my Ministry will form a workgroup to undertake a comprehensive review of the taking of informed consent by doctors.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The workgroup will also review the medical disciplinary process with a view to enhancing the regulatory framework.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This ranges from the filing of complaints to the structure, composition and processes of the Complaints Committees and the Disciplinary Tribunals and the use of expert evidence.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The workgroup will consult widely in evaluating the issues raised and make appropriate recommendations to the Ministry.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH will take into consideration these recommendations from the workgroup.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To ensure consistency and fairness in the sentencing of disciplinary cases, a separate committee, which is the Sentencing Guidelines Committee, was also appointed by the Singapore Medical Council in January 2019 to develop guidelines on the appropriate sanctions to be meted out.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: My Ministry will continue to engage the medical community and carefully consider what steps are necessary to improve the medical disciplinary process.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Minister Gan Kim Yong highlighted the need for all of us to work together to keep our healthcare system sustainable for future generations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: While MOH continues to provide subsidies, this will be unsustainable if we do not manage increases in healthcare costs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: A significant part of managing such increases is to aid patients and providers to choose care which is appropriate to the patient’s medical conditions and needs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Ms Joan Pereira has asked if we can explore having more subsidies for a wider range of generic drugs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Back in 2017, to encourage the use of generic drugs, we introduced a basket of clinically and cost-effective generic drugs which can replace the more expensive branded equivalents.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH reviews the generic drugs basket annually with the National Pharmacy and Therapeutics Committee.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will also actively monitor new generic drugs from overseas, and work with the Health Sciences Authority (HSA) to introduce them locally.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Currently, clinically and cost-effective drugs are eligible for subsidies.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: When generic alternatives of these subsidised drugs become available, prescribing of generic alternatives is encouraged to provide more savings for patients.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Ms Joan Pereira also asked about the Medication Assistance Fund (MAF), which was introduced to help needy patients pay for non-standard drugs which have been assessed to be clinically necessary.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since October 2018, MOH has streamlined the MAF application process such that eligible patients, with the assistance of hospital staff, can receive the MAF assistance upfront, without a separate financial assessment by the medical social worker.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The public hospitals will be enhancing their systems to support this simplified process.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To ensure costs are kept affordable, patients should also be informed of the estimated charges before making a decision.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Charles Chong has asked about the measures to empower patients to make informed decisions about private hospital fees.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since 2003, MOH has been publishing historical transacted hospital bill sizes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: More conditions were covered over the years and in 2014, we further published total operation fees for common procedures to ensure transparency of healthcare charges.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These fee benchmarks provide a useful reference to guide private healthcare providers in charging appropriately and enable patients and payers to make more informed decisions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Both the bill size publication and fee benchmarks are available on MOH's website.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Doctors should take reference from the benchmarks in setting their fees and advising their patients.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: They should also be prepared to explain to patients where their charges exceed the range, such as when addressing a highly complex case, or in exceptional circumstances.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Patients are encouraged to use the benchmarks to have a conversation with their doctor on their treatment, the complexity of their condition and the fees charged.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will monitor the bills and charging practice following the release of the fee benchmarks and consider the approach for periodic updating of the fee benchmarks to ensure they remain relevant and updated.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Mohamed Irshad has asked about having reduced co-payment for patients with IP riders who are treated at public hospitals.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Co-payment is a tenet of our healthcare financing framework that encourages prudent and appropriate use of healthcare services, both in the private as well as the public sectors.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This helps to ensure that healthcare costs and health insurance premiums remain affordable and sustainable for Singaporeans in the long term.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The co-payment amounts can be paid using MediSave, up to the applicable limits.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MediFund is also available for those who require assistance with their healthcare bills.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang has asked for an update on precision medicine research and implementation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, I am glad to inform Mr Low Thia Khiang that MOH's Health Regulation Group, together with the Genetic Testing Advisory Committee, introduced a Code of Practice for the Standards for the provision of clinical and laboratory genetic/genomic testing services in July 2018.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Code addresses key issues, such as the competency and training of personnel delivering the services, and the appropriateness in the ordering of genetic tests.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: An IT architecture is also being conceptualised to pool together, store and analyse the information from healthcare institutions in a robust and secure manner.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Precision medicine has been deployed in our public healthcare institutions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Currently, gene-editing involving human subjects is regulated under the Human Biomedical Research Act.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Research of a nature similar to that of the cited case in China is strictly controlled and cannot be conducted without the explicit approval from MOH.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As precision medicine is an emerging field, we will need to carefully consider many factors, such as ethical, legal and social implications, and weigh the investments required against the potential benefits, before systematically implementing the strategy to maximise the benefit to the population.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue our efforts to keep our healthcare system sustainable for the long term and ensure that all Singaporeans can receive appropriate and affordable care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Beyond keeping healthcare affordable, we need to keep Singapore and Singaporeans safe from infectious diseases.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH regularly reviews existing legislation, policies and capacity to safeguard public health and prevent the spread of infectious diseases.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Key amendments include strengthening processes for infectious disease notifications and surveillance, powers to disseminate health advisories more expediently, and enhancing powers for national public health research.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In addition to enhancing legislation, we have also increased public health education and protection by providing guidance on recommended vaccinations through the National Childhood Immunisation Schedule and the National Adult Immunisation Schedule.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked about the vaccination take-up rates.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Measles and diphtheria vaccination rates, at age two, have been around 95% or higher in the last decade.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The take-up of recommended vaccinations for adults has been encouraging, with more using MediSave for them.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, there is still room for improvement as the numbers represent a small proportion of the at-risk population for which vaccination is recommended.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH will continue to educate the public on the importance and benefits of vaccination to encourage up-take but, ultimately, we should all take responsibility for our own health by going for the recommended vaccinations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Minister Gan Kim Yong mentioned that MOH has developed the National Centre for Infectious Diseases (NCID), a 330-bed national facility designed for containment of dangerous infectious diseases.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It is expected to be fully operational by May 2019.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: During an outbreak, NCID will centrally manage the screening, isolation and treatment of infected patients.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: NCID also houses public health capabilities, such as the National Public Health Laboratory, to support the detection of infectious diseases.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We must work together as one to tackle the challenges and ensure that Singaporeans can enjoy many more years of health to come.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Chairman, the Minister for Health has emphasised in his speech earlier our collective responsibility in ensuring better health for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With a united front, I believe we can do much more, moving forward to ensure that healthcare remains sustainable, accessible and also affordable for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling asked how can we keep our healthcare affordable and sustainable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Pritam Singh also wanted to understand how we can pay for our hospitalisation bills that fall below the MediShield Life deductible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As a starting premise, our healthcare financing system is designed to ensure that no Singaporean is denied access to appropriate healthcare because they cannot pay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We provide support through multiple and often overlapping layers, each one playing an important but different role.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, all Singaporeans are covered by MediShield Life, for life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MediShield Life focuses on large bills and selected costly outpatient treatments to keep the premiums affordable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, we then have MediSave to help Singaporeans set aside part of their income to pay for future healthcare needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singaporeans can also tap on MediSave to pay for MediShield Life deductible and co-insurance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 2017, the majority of Singaporeans already pay little or no cash after subsidies, MediShield Life and MediSave for their subsidised hospitalisation bills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Nonetheless, we must continue to constantly innovate, raise productivity, manage cost and also be responsive to changes in order to ensure the long-term sustainability of our healthcare financing model.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling has also asked a broad question on how ready an average Singaporean might be, in terms of coping with his or her healthcare cost, especially in old age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Projections on expenses give us some assurance but we have to remember that healthcare costs can vary and can vary quite easily with a myriad of factors, such as personal health management, disease progression trends, medical technological advances and, of course, the effectiveness of our care model transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are, in turn, shaped by the actions of individuals, providers and payers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We, therefore, take a calibrated approach to regularly review and take stock, see where we are, and ensure that our financing schemes continue to be relevant and adequate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue to do so, to keep care affordable and accessible at each setting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the primary care setting, we have targeted subsidies at Singaporeans who need them more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: CHAS enables Singaporeans from lower- to middle-income households to receive subsidies at participating GPs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 2018, about 630,000 patients have benefited from reduced out-of-pocket medical expenses due to CHAS and are, therefore, better able to cope with their bills, especially for chronic conditions, such as diabetes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With an ageing population, we expect more Singaporeans will require assistance to help manage their chronic conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Primary care, being the foundational bedrock of our healthcare system, plays a critical role in shifting healthcare beyond hospitals and into the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We want Singaporeans to be able to obtain chronic care in the community, and to work with GPs in enabling that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have, therefore, reviewed our financing structure, to better achieve this, with the whole primary care sector and our partner GPs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is a major philosophical shift, as Singapore has never had universal subsidies for GP care, but we believe this will help Singaporeans as they grow old and also allow for a greater anchoring of chronic care in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And as Dr Lily Neo puts it, to facilitate the seeking of early treatment as far as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This new tier, CHAS Green, will soon be available to all Singaporeans who previously did not qualify for CHAS Blue or CHAS Orange.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition to keeping primary care affordable, CHAS will be another step towards transforming our primary care system to serve Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To better support existing CHAS cardholders as well in managing their chronic conditions, we will also be increasing the annual subsidies for complex chronic conditions for CHAS Blue and Orange cardholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They will see an increase of up to $20 in their annual subsidies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This means that existing CHAS cardholders can now enjoy up to $500 in annual chronic subsidies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will also be introducing additional subsidies for CHAS Orange cardholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They will be able to receive up to $10 in subsidy per visit for common illnesses, such as cough and cold, at CHAS GP clinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These changes will take place from 1 November 2019 onwards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will provide more details closer to that date.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To encourage more Singaporeans to tap on the scheme, my Ministry is also looking into ways to simplify the application process for CHAS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are developing an online application, which we expect to be ready by September 2019.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It will be more convenient for Singaporeans thereafter to apply and we hope that more Singaporeans can benefit from CHAS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, as CHAS helps more Singaporeans manage their chronic conditions at CHAS GPs near their home, we will put in the measures to monitor that CHAS clinics are, in fact, delivering good outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MOH is also reviewing clinical guidelines for care provided at CHAS dental clinics, to ensure that the care delivered is appropriate, relevant and meets the needs of the patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Aside from Government subsidies, we also review our MediSave limits regularly to keep subsidised healthcare affordable for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Muhamad Faisal Abdul Manap asked what are the considerations in determining the MediSave withdrawal limits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MediSave withdrawal limits are set to be sufficient for the vast majority of expenses in each healthcare setting, after Government subsidies and MediShield Life payouts, where applicable, are taken into account.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, for inpatient stays which MediSave is primarily designed for, we set different withdrawal limits to take into account the varying charges and also the different complexity of surgical procedures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MOH also considers the use of MediSave beyond withdrawal limits on a case-by-case basis, taking into account factors, such as the need for more complex treatments, sometimes unforeseen circumstances or complications, and also financial difficulties which may make it hard for the family to pay the outstanding bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ultimately, we need to strike a right balance between the present use of MediSave and its role as savings to cater for healthcare needs in old age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Dr Lily Neo asked about the affordability of long-term care and, more specifically, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh proposed increasing the MediSave withdrawal limits for such care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, we also enabled a cash withdrawal of up to $200 a month from MediSave to complement these schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And that is not too different from the median 59 months which is proposed by Assoc Prof Daniel Goh.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh's 60 months was premised on taking it out exactly, but we have to cater for individuals who might require the services beyond the immediate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The amount of MediSave withdrawal has been carefully considered to strike the right balance between the long-term care and other medical needs of an individual, such as insurance premiums and also hospitalisation expenses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Those who require further assistance beyond what I have mentioned can seek help from MediFund, ComCare and the upcoming Elderfund.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The long-term care needs of Singaporeans are, therefore, not solely reliant on a single measure like MediSave withdrawals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They are supported, in fact, by a robust long-term care financing framework that mirrors the current financing framework for acute care, which has worked well for us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These complications could give rise to large bills and become a worry for expectant parents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, who raised the point last year, asked for an update on the review.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Besides providing greater assurance against large hospitalisation bills, we also regularly review how MediShield Life can stay relevant as the model of care evolves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, on direct admissions into community hospitals which Mr Murali Pillai asked about and raised a suggestion earlier in the House to allow patients who were directly admitted into community hospitals to tap on to MediShield Life and MediSave, similar to those who were transferred from the acute hospitals for continuation of care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Patients identified for such direct admissions have to be reviewed to be in a stable condition with a clear diagnosis, and require a period of medical, nursing or rehabilitation care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Reason for that is because they are stepping down to a community hospital.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is to ensure that patients are appropriately right-sited and care is safe for patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: All patients in community hospitals can already tap on their MediSave, regardless of where they were admitted from.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue to review MediShield Life coverage for other direct admissions into community hospitals, based on assessment that such admission is appropriate and safe for patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, on bone marrow transplants, patients undergoing an autologous bone marrow transplant for multiple myeloma used to be admitted for the entire transplant treatment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Presently, however, part of the transplant treatment, including conditioning, stem cell infusion and post-transplant monitoring, can be done in an outpatient setting for suitable patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This potentially shortens the inpatient stays by up to three weeks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Treatment received in the inpatient setting will continue to be claimable under the existing inpatient claim limits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition to MediShield Life, we will soon introduce our second national insurance scheme, CareShield Life, next year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked for more transparency on the adequacy ratios and the assumptions behind premium pricing for these schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As a start, it must be remembered that MediShield Life and CareShield Life are not-for-profit, long-term schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Collected premiums and the investment returns are solely used for the administration of the scheme and the benefit of policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There is no other use of these funds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Premiums are priced by external professional actuaries based on established actuarial principles, taking into account scheme benefits, claims experience, and future changes in demographics, utilisation rates and, of course, the costs of medical treatment, amongst other factors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For MediShield Life, the actual claims experience has been close to the projections used in the pricing of premiums.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But we have to bear in mind that these are current-year claims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As MediShield Life, however, is a long-term scheme, and part of the premiums collected are set aside as reserves to support long-term commitments and to buffer against adverse scenarios, such as a worse than expected claims experience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Further, to help with the affordability of premiums in advanced years, policyholders also pay ahead during their working ages, so that their premiums rise by less in their older ages, when, at that stage, they become less economically active.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Quite apart from that, we also regularly monitor the capital adequacy ratio and the incurred loss ratio of the fund to ensure that the Fund remains healthy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The capital adequacy ratio reflects the Scheme's ability to meet its liabilities under adverse scenarios.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MediShield Life's capital adequacy ratio for 2017 falls within the range of private healthcare insurers'.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As part of our ongoing review of the MediShield Life claims limit, we will also be reviewing the scheme's capital adequacy ratio in tandem with its impact on premiums.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This ratio compares the total premiums collected to the total monies required to ensure that the Fund is able to meet both current-year claims and also its liabilities into the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Total monies required for the Fund include immediate claims payout each year, and the change in required reserves for future payouts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A less appropriate approach sometimes cited to assess the adequacy of the Fund's premiums collection is to compare total premiums collected to total claims paid in the same year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This approach, however, is not a holistic representation as it omits a large part of what MediShield Life's premiums are meant to support, namely, future long-term claims and premium affordability in advanced ages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For MediShield Life, the benefits are outlined in the information booklet issued to all members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Further information about the Fund size, the reserves and the Incurred Loss Ratio is published on the MOH website, and the MediShield Life financial accounts are audited each year by an external auditor and then submitted to Parliament every year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, the independent MediShield Life Council also reviews premiums collection and claims experience amongst others, and thereafter provides recommendations to the Government to ensure that MediShield Life provides effective protection in an affordable and sustainable manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The CareShield Life scheme design was also discussed in this House in 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: CareShield Life supports the long-term care needs of Singaporeans in old age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Premiums are paid during the working ages for lifetime coverage should the policyholder become disabled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Similar to MediShield Life, an independent CareShield Life Council will be set up to advise the Government on the sustainability of the CareShield Life scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I turn now to address the questions and the cuts on caregiver support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Even as we address Singaporeans' concern over healthcare expenses, we also recognise the need to consider accessibility to healthcare, which is critical for the timely management of the condition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is especially so for the elderly who needs long-term care, and we must also care for the caregiver.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With this in mind, MOH announced a Caregiver Support Action Plan earlier last month to strengthen support for senior caregiving.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling and Mr Charles Chong have asked what we intend to do to continue to support caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We intend to do more in at least three areas – financial support, FWAs and options for respite care for caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: While the FDW Grant helps to offset the costs of hiring an FDW, the HCG provides greater flexibility to help offset more caregiving expenses, such as the costs of home and community-based services, and transportation to medical appointments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In some cases, some might prefer to hire an FDW to help; others might not; it does not matter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The HCG can be used in either scenario.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will help working caregivers to manage their work and caregiving commitments and is a key step to building a sustainable approach that balances the needs of both employers and employees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, we will be expanding the existing respite care services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We currently have respite services at our centres and nursing homes to allow caregivers to take a break from their caregiving duties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Centre-based respite services cater to the needs of caregivers who need a few hours off, while nursing home respite services allow overnight stays from several days to a few weeks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue to explore new models of care to meet the needs of caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Caregiver Support Action Plan complements the already existing suite of services and schemes currently available to seniors and their caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MOH will be implementing the Action Plan over the next two years to better support caregivers and will provide more details on other specific measures in the coming months.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Further to strengthening the financial and caregiving support, we also believe that having a reliable healthcare network is fundamental to every successful healthcare system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And this could be achieved through proper regulations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Prof Fatimah Lateef has asked for an update on our regulatory approach and progress with the regulatory sandbox.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As a regulator, our priority is with ensuring patient safety and proper continuity of care, as new and innovative care models evolve to meet the healthcare needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To do so effectively and safely, there is a need to review and replace the current Private Hospitals and Medical Clinics Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To complement the change in our approach to regulation, we have also launched a regulatory sandbox in April last year to support the safe growth of new modalities of care and innovations within current care services, that is, the Licensing Experimentation and Adaptation Programme (LEAP).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Doctor-led telemedicine and house calls were the first services to come under LEAP and, within the last year, we have 11 providers on LEAP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As providers and models mature, we are also encouraging a shift in the services provided, from managing simple acute conditions, such as cough and cold, to more complex chronic diseases, such as diabetes, supporting MOH's "Beyond Hospital to Community" strategy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Prof Fatimah Lateef will be pleased to note, and I think Mr Leon Perera also raised the point about encouraging innovation in the intermediate and long-term care sector, that we are constantly looking at how technology can help us create a sustainable healthcare future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are also supporting our healthcare institutions to find solutions to increase productivity through the Healthcare Productivity Fund.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, even with innovations in modalities of care and changes in the way patients can access healthcare services with technology, we are mindful that there are certain aspects of care that we should not or perhaps ought not to replace, for example, the human touch.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One of our key strategies in supporting productivity is to continually explore how innovations can free up manpower from routine work so that they can go back to the business of caring for patients directly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To conclude, Chairman, the Government will continue to support productivity and innovation for greater healthcare sustainability, affordability and accessibility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We hope that new policies, such as the enhanced CHAS scheme, will encourage all Singaporeans to seek help early and in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will also be helping caregivers to continue to care for their loved ones in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Let us all work together and move away from healthcare to health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With each and every one of us taking good care of our health, we can all be hopefully happy and active in our golden years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Mr Chairman, I will focus on three areas: removing trans fat from our food supply; reducing smoking rates; and third, strengthening our health ecosystem.
